title: Microsoft just shared Azure’s actual revenue in dollars: $33.2 billion
content:
Microsoft has never disclosed Azure’s quarterly revenue in dollars. It has typically only shared a growth percentage or described revenue dollar milestones in vague ways. But on Wednesday, when it posted another record-breaking quarter, it reported that Azure brought in a healthy $33.2 billion in revenue for the July–September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier.
The disclosure lets investors line up Azure’s performance more directly against Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, whose parent companies already report cloud revenue in dollars every quarter.
Alphabet, which also reported earnings on Wednesday, said Google Cloud brought in $30.7 billion in the same quarter, putting Azure slightly ahead. But Google Cloud, which also includes Google’s Workspace subscriptions, roughly doubled its revenue from a year earlier, growing about twice as fast as Azure, according to TechCrunch’s calculations.
Azure, where businesses rent computing power to run applications, SaaS, and to build and run AI models, is now Microsoft’s largest and fastest-growing product line by the company’s own figures. It accounted for roughly 36% of Microsoft’s $92.3 billion in quarterly revenue.
Azure’s revenue was also about $850 million more than the $32.3 billion analysts expected. Azure’s 48% growth rate also topped the 44% to 45% that Microsoft CFO Amy Hood forecast on the company’s July earnings call.
Azure sits inside Agents and Infra, one of two new business segments Microsoft introduced this quarter. Microsoft previously reported three segments, Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud and More Personal Computing. The new Agents and Infra segment, which groups Azure with Microsoft 365’s cloud business, brought in $76.8 billion, up 25% from a year earlier.
Amazon reports its earnings on Thursday. Analysts also expect its cloud, Amazon Web Services, to grow. It’s been the largest cloud since the beginning of time and no one expects Microsoft to best it right now. But with all of them reporting actual dollars, the race is on.

report.summary: Microsoft disclosed Azure’s quarterly revenue for the first time: $33.2 billion, up 48%, making cloud AI spending and competition more measurable.
report.background: Cloud providers have long reported growth rates or vague milestones rather than absolute quarterly revenue, which made direct comparisons difficult for investors and buyers. Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud already disclose dollar figures, so Microsoft’s new detail changes the scoreboard. The disclosure comes as AI workloads drive demand for rented computing power, model training and inference, and enterprise software. Microsoft also reorganized reporting into new segments, grouping Azure with Microsoft 365 cloud in “Agents and Infra.” Azure is now central to Microsoft’s AI strategy and overall growth, so its revenue is a key signal of whether AI infrastructure spending is translating into cloud sales.
key_points: Azure generated $33.2 billion in the July–September quarter, up 48% year over year. That beat the roughly $32.3 billion analysts expected and topped Microsoft CFO Amy Hood’s 44%–45% growth forecast, suggesting AI-related cloud demand remained stronger than the company had guided.

Google Cloud reported $30.7 billion in the same quarter, putting Azure slightly ahead in raw dollars. But Google Cloud, which includes Workspace subscriptions, grew about twice as fast as Azure, so the headline dollar comparison does not capture the full competitive picture.

Azure accounted for roughly 36% of Microsoft’s $92.3 billion quarterly revenue and is now Microsoft’s largest and fastest-growing product line by its own figures. The new Agents and Infra segment, which includes Azure and Microsoft 365 cloud, brought in $76.8 billion, up 25%.

The disclosure gives investors a cleaner way to compare Azure with AWS and Google Cloud. AWS reports earnings the next day and is still expected to be the largest cloud, but with all three reporting actual dollars, the race becomes more directly measurable.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Microsoft’s disclosure turns cloud revenue into a clearer benchmark for AI infrastructure demand, capital spending and monetization. It may pressure rivals to be more transparent and help investors judge whether AI hype is producing real cloud sales. For developers, more visible competition could mean sharper pricing, regional capacity battles and faster tooling improvements, though cost management remains essential. For regular users, the main effect is indirect: stronger cloud competition can support more capable AI features, better reliability and possibly lower prices over time. Enterprise buyers also gain more leverage when comparing providers on actual scale and growth, not just marketing claims.
report.tools: To follow cloud AI economics, watch cloud pricing calculators from Azure, AWS and Google Cloud, plus open-source cost tools such as OpenCost and Kubecost for Kubernetes spending, Infracost for infrastructure-as-code estimates, and Cloud Custodian for governance. For AI workloads, Azure AI Foundry, vLLM, Ray and KServe are useful for experimenting with model serving and scaling while tracking cost and performance.
